newsitem.title: GERMANY: German firms suffer new round of worker protests.
newsitem.headline: German firms suffer new round of worker protests.

text.p: Germany's key metal and engineering industries suffered more disruption on Monday as hundreds of thousands of workers staged new protests against a law aimed at cutting sick pay allowances.

IG Metall, Germany's most powerful union, said that around 400,000 workers in over 1,000 metal and engineering firms across the country had downed tools during the day, with many then going on to march through major towns.

The protests followed the break-down on Wednesday of talks between IG Metall and metal employers seeking compromise on the sick pay issue. They went ahead despite pledges by companies such as Daimler-Benz to hold off implementing the law.

Around 120,000 engineering workers organised stoppages earlier this month when the law, which cuts sick pay to 80 percent of salary from 100 percent, first came in. Production losses then were estimated at hundreds of millions of marks.
German's North-Rhine Westphalia steel-producing region took the brunt of the latest wave of protests, with unions estimating more than 160,000 participants in demonstrations.
Steel furnaces run by top German steel producers including Thyssen AG and Krupp-Hoesch Stahl were hit by stoppages that started in the night-shift of Wednesday night and went on through the day.

IG Metall said that furnaces at Duisburg, Bochum and Dortmund had been put on emergency running levels due to walk-outs and that protest marches had taken part in major industrial towns including the state capital Duesseldorf.
Luxury car-maker Mercedes, whose parent Daimler was the main target of the earlier wave of protests after it tried unsuccessfully to implement the sick pay cuts immediately, again suffered heavily.

Some 800 passenger cars and 100 lorries were not built as a result of the stoppages, which included a walk-out by 15,000 workers at its largest passenger car plant in Sindelfingen near Stuttgart, according to union estimates.
Other firms hit by the protests included Volkswagen AG's Audi car-making unit, electronics group Robert Bosch GmbH and Alcatel Alsthom's Alcatel SEL telecom arm.

Union officials said employers had brought the disruption on themselves with their continued insistence that labour costs in Germany must fall and criticised the government for siding with industry on the issue.

"The responsibility for all this lies completely with the hardliners in the government and among the employers," said Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy chairman of the DGB trade union umbrella organisation.
Gesamtmetall, which had been leading the collapsed talks on Wednesday, said the unrest not only caused huge production losses but "lasting damage to Germany as a place for industry".

IG Metall and Gesamtmetall had been seeking a compromise between cuts to non-wage labour costs that employers are demanding and IG Metall's insistence that companies offer firm pledges on job protection in the 1997 pay round.
But discussions foundered as no agreement could be reached on the issue of sick pay cuts, a move that would save German business some 12 billion marks ($7.88 billion) a year.

Firms including Daimler, General Motors Opel and Siemens AG have, as a result of the earlier protests, said they would hold off implementing the new sick pay law until contractual agreement with unions had been reached.
They are certain, however, to seek to introduce the new law into new wage contracts after the current ones run out at the end of the year. ($1=1.5230 Mark)
